How to separate ingredient, dish, and technique clues

Phoodle runs on three distinct word types, and conflating them is where most solve paths stall out. Ingredients are the raw materials: flour, lemon, basil. Dishes are combinations that carry cultural weight: risotto, paella, consommé. Techniques are the actions and processes: braise, julienne, deglaze. The hint system on this page tends to label one of these categories explicitly if you tap it twice, which narrows your field considerably.

When the hint says "technique," your brain should pivot immediately to verbs and methods. When it points toward dish, think proper nouns and regional associations. Mixing these up leads to wasting guesses on perfectly valid words that happen to be the wrong category—a frustration that's easy to avoid once the pattern clicks.

Where familiar food words become the wrong guess

Sauté and sautéed look identical to most solvers, but Phoodle treats them differently depending on the clue structure. The same goes for broth versus stock, and glaze versus icing. These near-synonyms trip up even experienced players because they're semantically close while being categorically distinct in the game's logic.

The reveal card on today's page shows the answer uses a spelling variant that eliminates several plausible alternatives. Spelling matters more here than it does in standard crosswords. If you're stuck between caramelize and caramelise, check which version appears in the clue text—that's your tiebreaker.

The recent history tab shows your last five answers. Players who notice their error patterns perform measurably better on subsequent puzzles.
